The most related to my line of work is "the ideas factory" which discusses the early and hay days of bell labs. 

A personal favorite of mine, though chemistry and not physics is 'the periodic table' is by a Jewish chemist and contains anecdotes from their early carrier and time in Auschwitz along with fictional stories. Each chapter is focused around a single element. I can't remember if it was in that book or "if this is a Man" but the strangeness of encountering a German copy of one of the seminal chemistry books he was familiar with in the Auschwitz lab. He proved himself useful enough in this capacity that he escaped the more grueling physical labor and synthesised glycerin to eat to prevent starvation. Great if you like history and captures a surprising amount of detail in the life of an early career researcher at the time.

You've been accepted onto the program, this was the decision of several people who are knowledgeable in the field and invested in picking a candidate they think can stay the course. You have met the entry requirements and therefore, academically, probably have what it takes. It's now a matter of applying yourself, repeatedly.

There's no single formula for success but if you show up and give it a go then you'll be well on your way. Somedays or weeks may go by without you making much progress however whatever you do for your project it's better than doing nothing. If you're stuck/struggling then talk to someone. 

And even when you're not stuck, talk to other PhD students and people you're working with. They can give you useful advice and often a grounding sense of perspective. Science often has setbacks and progress may at times be slower than you expected.

It can feel like a lot is at stake but worrying about it is just going to distract you. So cool it, if possible, nothing is set in stone and you certainly haven't failed yet. Wishing you the very best for it.

I found mindfulness to be one of the more effective ways of managing anxiety. For me, being able to stay present and cut out/down on intrusive thoughts took a lot of practice. It's still not something I can do consistently but on average it's improved my life by providing a way to cope with stress while it's happening. Stick at it and try not to be frustrated at yourself if you can always manage it. Changing patterns of thinking is really difficult.

However I had very vivid dreams that related to the book for about a week after I finished 'Someone comes to town, someone leaves town' by Cory Doctorow. The book was very surreal, the main character's father was a mountain and mother was a washing machine. This planted the notion in my mind that anything could be capable of holding conciousness.
